text:
The reason SSDs wear out comes down to how flash memory holds data. A cell stores information as electrical charge, trapped either in a floating gate or in a charge-trap layer, and to write or erase it, the drive has to push electrons through a thin layer of insulating oxide. Each program/erase cycle does a bit of damage to that oxide. Eventually the cell can't hold its charge well enough for the drive to tell one voltage level from another. TLC (triple-level cell) flash packs three bits into every cell, which means its voltages have to be precise, and it usually lasts for only around 3,000 cycles.

In practice, that number goes further than you'd think, because drives are built to stretch it. The controller uses wear leveling to distribute writes across all the blocks, so one area doesn't wear out early while others go untouched. This holds even if you keep rewriting the same file. Over-provisioning also helps. Manufacturers commonly set aside about 7% of the raw capacity as spare space that the user never sees. The controller draws on it to shuffle data during garbage collection, reduce unnecessary writes, and replace worn blocks with fresh ones. With all of this in place, a typical SSD can handle years of normal use.
